public_rationale: The transparency-pledge component holds: the July announcement names seven leading companies and includes public-reporting commitments. The categorical claim that none disclosed dataset contents is too broad under the ordinary source-level reading. Microsoft's June phi-1 paper identified source datasets, synthetic components, quantities, and preparation methods. However, such disclosure is not a complete training-corpus release. Llama 2's documentation illustrates the limited detail behind Marcus's concern. The result therefore depends on the distinction between substantive source disclosure and full inspectability.
limitations: Phi-1 is a specialized coding model; it would not settle a claim expressly restricted to the largest general-purpose frontier models.
The cited disclosures do not establish access to every training document.
The pledge evidence is an archival reproduction of an official announcement.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: None of the big AI companies discloses what is in their training data sets despite pledging transparency.

statement.excerpt: The big companies have all pledged fealty to transparency, but none of them will actually tells us what’s in their data sets.
statement.document_title: Six months after the Pause letter, AI is still erratic — and still something we should still be deeply concerned about

from_speaker: have all pledged fealty to transparency
our_interpretation: The transparency-pledge reference is read in the context of the White House commitments discussed in the post.

The ordinary reading of disclosing what is in a dataset includes substantive information about named sources and composition. A generic description such as publicly available material provides much less information.
The wording does not explicitly restrict the claim to each company's newest frontier model, or require publication of every training document.
Source-level disclosure and a complete, independently inspectable training corpus are assessed separately.
No measurement period is specified. I use the six-month retrospective named in the title, ending on publication, as the reporting window.
criteria.support_condition: The relevant major companies made transparency pledges, while their disclosures provided no substantive identification of training-data constituents.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A relevant major company published substantive source or composition information for an AI training dataset, or the claimed transparency pledges were absent.

evidence.publisher: The White House, reproduced by the American Presidency Project
evidence.explanation: The archived official announcement names Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Inflection, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI as participants in transparency-related commitments. Those commitments do not themselves require publication of training-corpus contents.

evidence.excerpt: filtered code-language corpus and synthetic textbooks
evidence.locator: Section 2.3, Pretraining; dataset construction described in Sections 2–2.2
evidence.explanation: The paper identifies filtered material from The Stack and StackOverflow, synthetic textbooks, and generated exercises, with quantities and preparation methods. This is substantive disclosure by a major pledge participant, though it does not release every training example.

Llama 2's pretraining description supplies broad provenance and filtering information without identifying a complete source inventory. It supports the narrower concern about limited inspectability, but cannot establish what every major company disclosed.
The original LLaMA paper names datasets and describes source proportions and filtering. It predates the target window and concerns LLaMA rather than Llama 2, so it is contextual counterevidence only.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A specified company and model set, plus a stated disclosure threshold, would allow a firmer assessment of the narrower frontier-training-data claim.
